sampling_plan.purpose: Map the source’s chapter progression and separate foundational technique from later subject applications.
Test line/ellipse drills and Robertson’s viewing-position model against existing eye-level and convergence cards.
Compare subdivision, mirroring, and curve-transfer methods to D’Amelio plane metrology and existing perspective construction.
Inspect grid construction, off-page VPs, rotated same-scale grids, underlays, and grid-model tradeoffs for new capabilities.
Inspect ellipse/rotation diagrams and resolve the prior Norling/White ellipse-axis verification hold as far as Robertson supports it.
Test X-Y-Z section drawing and surface projection as a potential Deep capability rather than a collection of small tricks.
Check environments, aircraft, wheeled vehicles, wide-angle grids, and media chapters for late unique perspective deltas.

observations.summary: The book is deliberately cumulative: craft and perspective terminology lead to grids, ellipses, X-Y-Z volumes, then environment/vehicle applications. Later chapters mostly apply the earlier machinery.

Viewing-position terminology reframes existing camera logic with Station Point, Line of Sight, Picture Plane, and Cone of Vision; the line and ellipse exercises are valuable short activations rather than new perspective theory.
Rectangle division, multiplication, mirroring, and curve transfer substantially reinforce D’Amelio/White plane metrology; no separate duplicate cards are warranted.

Two genuine operational deltas survive: preserving unit scale across rotated grids, and constructing coherent local grids when VPs lie off the page. Underlay and grid-type sections also strengthen scene/distortion workflows.
Robertson strongly supports minor-axis control for practical ellipse placement and rotations, but the universal mathematical scope remains unresolved against the prior exact-circle construction.

X-Y-Z section drawing is a major new volume-construction workflow. The chapter builds forms from draft views, perspective profiles, cross-sections, tangent silhouettes, cuts, and projected surface curves.

Environment, aircraft, and vehicle chapters validate the portability of grids and section drawing; most are domain applications. Wide-angle/fisheye examples create a later mathematical audit queue rather than immediate universal rules.

rationale: Robertson overlaps a mature perspective foundation but clearly contains new construction workflows that cannot be judged from samples alone, especially the grid and X-Y-Z volume chapters. Full reading is required to separate durable methods from vehicle/environment examples and numeric camera heuristics.
